title: Age — The Invisible Man
hook: Somewhere after sixty, many men notice that people start talking past them, and the body that once commanded a room is now walked around.
why:
Ageing changes how a man's body is read long before it changes who he is. Lines and folds make a resting face look sad or stern. A slower walk is taken as a slower mind. Hearing loss is mistaken for confusion. And as a man leaves work, loses friends and perhaps a partner, he can find himself on the edge of conversations he once led, spoken to slowly and loudly by people half his age.

Most men will live this from the inside, and almost every man will read it from the outside: in a father, a neighbour, a colleague near retirement, a patient, a customer. The misreadings matter. They shape how older men are treated by doctors, employers and families, and there is good evidence that what older people come to believe about age gets into their bodies and their health.

This chapter covers how older faces are misread, why older people are literally seen less, the habit of elderspeak, hearing loss, what a slower walk does and does not mean, how beliefs about age affect health, and the quiet withdrawal that loneliness produces in older men.

teach.p:
As faces age, the skin loses elasticity and lines form along the paths that expressions have travelled for decades: folds from the nose to the corners of the mouth, creases at the eyes, furrows across the brow. Many of these resemble the shapes of emotional expressions. Corners of the mouth that sag a little at rest can look like sadness; vertical lines between the brows can look like a frown.

Researchers have tested what this does to observers. In 2012 Ursula Hess, Reginald Adams and colleagues showed that the wrinkles and folds of older faces make their expressions less clear, so that even a clear expression on an older face tends to be read as mixed. In 2015 Maxi Freudenberg, Hess and colleagues found that neutral expressions were rated as more emotional on older faces than on younger ones, both by people and by an automated recognition system. Expressions on older faces are also recognised less accurately overall.

In everyday terms, an older man sitting quietly may be read as sad, disapproving or grumpy when he is simply resting. A smile may land as less warm than he means it. Over time, being misread like this can change how people approach him, and how much they bother to.

The figure here sits at rest, hands on his thighs, face in repose. Nothing in his mood is on display. Before deciding that an older man is low or annoyed, listen to his voice and words, and compare his face with how it looks on a day you know was good.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if neutral older faces were read as accurately as younger ones. Hess, Freudenberg and colleagues found that ageing faces are read as more emotional at rest and less clear when expressing, so misreadings are common.
teach.pullQuote: An older man sitting quietly may be read as sad or grumpy when he is simply resting.

teach.p:
Older people often describe a strange experience: becoming invisible. Shop assistants serve the younger customer behind them. In a group, the conversation turns away from them. Research offers part of an explanation. People are better at recognising faces from their own age group, an effect known as the own-age bias, documented across many studies in a 2012 review by Matthew Rhodes and Jeffrey Anastasi. Younger adults pay less attention to older faces, look at them less and remember them less well.

Social life adds to the effect. A working man's job gives him a role in many conversations: he is the one people ask, the one who decides, the one who knows. Retirement removes that role overnight. Without it, an older man in a group of younger people can find himself at the edge of the circle, nodding along, rarely addressed.

Being seen less has a body. Men who feel overlooked often stop offering opinions, stand a little further back, and speak more briefly, which makes them easier still to overlook. What looks like reserve may be the result of years of small exclusions.

The figures here stand in a loose circle, an older man among two younger colleagues, all turned toward the shared centre. Including someone is mostly a matter of bodies: turning to face him, leaving him a gap, looking at him when you ask a question of the group, and waiting for his answer as long as you would wait for anyone else's.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if people attended equally to faces of all ages. The own-age bias shows that younger adults recognise and attend to older faces less well than to faces of their own age.

teach.p:
Elderspeak is the name researchers such as Susan Kemper have given to a way of talking to older people as if they were children. It is slower, louder and simpler than ordinary speech, with exaggerated, sing-song intonation, short sentences, repetition, terms of endearment such as dear or young man, and the collective we: are we ready for our tablets? It is often meant kindly. It is usually heard as patronising.

Its effects can be measured. In a 2009 study, Kristine Williams and her colleagues analysed videotaped care in nursing homes for people with dementia. Residents were about twice as likely to resist care, by pulling away, refusing or becoming agitated, after staff used elderspeak than after ordinary adult talk. Even people with dementia heard the difference, and responded to it with their bodies.

Elderspeak has a nonverbal side too: leaning over someone, patting a hand or a shoulder uninvited, talking to the companion rather than the older person, smiling the fixed smile adults use with small children. It turns an adult conversation into a performance of care.

The alternative is plain: speak to an older man as you would to any adult. Use his name, not a pet name. Speak at a normal pace and a clear volume. Ask rather than announce. The figures here sit across a table, each looking at the other; she is talking to him, at his level, as one adult to another.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if older people responded to elderspeak as they do to ordinary talk. Williams and colleagues found that residents with dementia resisted care about twice as often after elderspeak.

teach.p:
Hearing loss is one of the most common conditions of later life. The World Health Organization estimates that more than a quarter of people over sixty have a disabling hearing loss, and men are affected earlier and more often than women. Many do not use hearing aids, through cost, pride or simply not noticing how much they miss.

The behaviour that results is easy to misread. A man who cannot follow a conversation in a noisy room may nod along, smile at the wrong moment, answer a question that was not asked, or withdraw into silence. Others may read this as confusion, early dementia, rudeness or lack of interest. He may simply have heard every third word.

Hearing loss also changes posture. People who are hard of hearing often lean in, turn one ear toward the speaker, tilt the head or watch the speaker's mouth closely. These are signs of effort, not of suspicion or intrusiveness.

Helping is mostly a matter of position. Face him, so that he can see your mouth. Sit where the light falls on your face rather than behind you. Move away from background noise. Speak clearly at a normal pace; shouting distorts speech and drawing out words makes them harder to read on the lips. If he has not understood, rephrase rather than repeating the same words louder. The figure here tilts his head, the posture of someone working to catch what is said.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if hearing loss in later life were rare or easy to spot. It is common, often untreated, and its signs are easily mistaken for confusion or disinterest.

teach.p:
Walking changes with age. Steps shorten, speed falls, the arms swing less, and many older men walk with a slightly wider base for balance. Walking speed is a genuine health signal: in 2011 Stephanie Studenski and her colleagues pooled nine studies of about 34,000 people over sixty-five and found that faster walking speed was linked to longer survival, with each tenth of a metre per second associated with a lower risk of death. Doctors increasingly treat gait speed as a vital sign.

But it is a signal about the body, not the mind or the man. Observers often take a slower, careful walk as a sign of frailty in every sense, and begin to treat the walker as less capable, less informed and less worth consulting. Spread, described in the previous chapter, applies to age as well as disability.

Walking with an older man is a small test of respect. Matching his pace, rather than walking half a step ahead and waiting, keeps the conversation shared. Not hovering at his elbow, unless he asks, leaves him his dignity. Mentioning a change in his walking is worth doing, privately and as a health matter, since a sudden slowing can be an early sign of illness.

The figures here walk side by side, a son beside his father, at the older man's pace and turned toward him as they talk. Nobody is leading.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if a slow walk said as much about the mind as about the body. Gait speed tracks physical health and survival; it says nothing on its own about what a man knows, thinks or can decide.

teach.h: What we believe gets into the body.
teach.p:
In 2002 Becca Levy and her colleagues analysed the Ohio Longitudinal Study of Aging and Retirement, which had asked 660 people aged fifty and over about their views of their own ageing, then followed them for up to twenty-three years. Those with more positive views of ageing lived about seven and a half years longer than those with more negative views, even after age, sex, income, loneliness and health were taken into account.

Levy's group has also tested whether stereotypes reach the body directly. In a 1999 study with Jeffrey Hausdorff and Jeanne Wei, older people exposed to positive words about ageing, flashed too quickly to be consciously seen, walked faster and with steadier steps afterwards. That study was small, and priming studies of this kind have had a mixed record when repeated, so it is best treated as suggestive rather than settled. The longevity findings rest on firmer, larger data.

The implication matters for anyone who deals with older men. The way they are treated, and the beliefs about age that they absorb from it, may affect how they hold themselves, how much they move and how long they live. A man who is constantly helped, slowed down and talked down to may begin to move and speak as if he were frailer than he is.

The figure here walks with a cane, head up, at his own pace. How he carries himself is partly his body and partly what he has come to believe about men of his age.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if beliefs about ageing had no link to health. Levy and colleagues found that positive self-perceptions of ageing predicted about seven and a half years of extra life, after controlling for health and other factors.

teach.p:
Many men rely on work and a partner for most of their social contact. When work ends and a partner dies or falls ill, the network can shrink quickly, and research on later life repeatedly finds widowers among the most isolated people of all. The health stakes are high: in a 2010 analysis of 148 studies, Julianne Holt-Lunstad and her colleagues found that people with stronger social relationships had about a fifty per cent greater likelihood of survival over the study periods.

Loneliness in older men is often hard to see, partly because men are less likely to name it. It shows in the body and in habits: fewer outings, letting appearance go, curt answers on the phone, irritability, staying in the same chair all day, or a sudden burst of talk when someone visits. Gruffness is easily read as bad temper and left alone, which deepens the isolation.

Approaches that work for many men are side by side rather than face to face. The Men's Sheds movement, which began in Australia and has spread to many countries, gives older men a workshop to share, with projects to work on together; conversation follows the work. A walk, a match, a job in the garden or a repair often opens more than a direct question about how he is feeling.

The figures here work side by side on a shared task. For many older men, that is the easiest posture in which to be close.
teach.disconfirm: This would be wrong if social connection made little difference to health in later life. Holt-Lunstad and colleagues found that stronger relationships were linked to substantially greater survival across 148 studies.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Leaving him at the edge of the group
poseGallery.annotation: Turn to face him, leave him a gap, and look at him when you ask the group a question.
Matching his pace keeps the conversation shared. Hovering at his elbow, unasked, does not.

poseGallery.dontCaption: Talking about him to his daughter
poseGallery.annotation: Speak to an older man as you would to any adult, at a normal pace, using his name.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side, adult to adult
poseGallery.dontCaption: Talking to him like a child
poseGallery.annotation: Elderspeak is heard as patronising, even by people with dementia. Use the voice and words you would use with any adult.

poseGallery.doCaption: Side by side on a shared task
poseGallery.dontCaption: Alone in the same chair all day
poseGallery.annotation: Many older men find company easier with a reason. A job that needs two people opens doors a visit cannot.

caseStudy:
Frank, seventy-four, was an electrician for forty years and has been a widower for two. His daughter, Helen, began going to his medical appointments with him after a fall. Within a few months she noticed that the doctors addressed almost everything to her, and that her father had stopped answering. At the pharmacy, a young assistant called him young man and explained his new tablets slowly, twice, in a voice usually kept for toddlers.

At family dinners Frank had gone quiet. He nodded along, laughed a beat late, and once answered a question about his grandson's football with a remark about the weather. Helen's husband wondered aloud whether it was the start of dementia.

It was his grandson, Sam, who noticed that Frank always sat with his back to the window, his face in shadow and everyone else's in glare, and that he leaned toward whoever was speaking with his head turned to one side. A hearing test found significant loss in both ears.

With hearing aids and a seat facing the light, Frank's conversation came back. Helen changed her own habits at appointments: when a doctor turned to her, she turned to her father and waited, and the doctor followed. Sam started taking Frank to a Men's Shed near his house, where he now spends two mornings a week fixing donated bicycles and arguing about wiring with a retired plumber.

Frank says the hearing aids helped, but what helped most was people looking at him again when they talked.
observe: Notice, in your next group conversation that includes an older man, how often he is addressed and how long people wait for his answers.
Notice any change in your own voice, pace or vocabulary when you speak to someone much older than you.
Notice how older men you know hold themselves in a noisy room: where they sit, which way they lean, how often they speak.
Notice how a resting older face strikes you, and whether you assume a mood from it.

drills.name: Adult to Adult
steps: Think of an older man you speak to regularly: a father, neighbour, colleague or customer.
Recall the last conversation, and note your pace, volume and the words you used.
Mark anything that would sound odd if said to a man of forty.
In your next conversation, speak to him exactly as you would to that man of forty.
variations: Record a voice note to an older relative and listen back for any change in pace, volume or vocabulary compared with a note to a friend.
Notice how shop and café staff speak to older customers this week, and whether any use elderspeak.
Ask an older man you know whether people ever talk down to him, and listen to the examples.

drills.name: Set Up the Room
steps: Before your next family meal or meeting with an older man, look at where everyone will sit.
Give him a seat facing the light, away from music, kitchens or traffic.
Sit where he can see your face, and speak clearly without raising your voice.
If he misses something, rephrase it rather than repeating it louder.
Afterwards, note how much he joined in compared with usual.
variations: Before the meal, ask him where he would like to sit, rather than deciding for him.
Turn off the background music or television during conversation, and notice the difference for everyone at the table.
If he wears hearing aids, ask whether a particular room or seat works best for them.

drills.name: Walk at His Pace
steps: Go for a walk with an older man you know.
Let him set the pace, and stay beside him rather than half a step ahead.
Turn your head toward him when you talk, as you would with anyone.
Notice how the conversation feels compared with talking while you lead.
variations: On the walk, ask him about a place you pass that he remembers from years ago, and let him tell the story at his own pace.
Walk the same route at your usual pace alone, then at his pace with him, and notice what you see on the slower walk that you missed on the faster.
Notice whether other people on the pavement walk round him or hurry past, and how he responds to it.

drills.name: Side by Side
steps: Think of an older man you know who seems to have withdrawn.
Choose a task you could do together: a repair, a garden job, a match, a walk.
Invite him to it, without making it about his loneliness.
Let the conversation come from the task rather than forcing it.
Repeat it, since one visit rarely changes much.
variations: Ask him to teach you something he knows, such as a repair, a recipe or a game, which turns the task into his expertise.
Choose a task that needs two people, such as moving furniture or putting up shelves, so that his help is genuinely needed.
Make it a regular arrangement, such as the first Saturday of every month, so that he can look forward to it.

quiz.q: A colleague says that an older man in your team must be unhappy, because his face looks sad whenever he is not talking. What does this chapter suggest?
options: He is probably right, since a sad face at rest is a reliable sign of an unhappy mood in older men
Lines and folds can make a resting older face look sad, so judge his mood from his words and voice
Older men hide their feelings completely, so nothing can be learned from them in any way at all
He is probably depressed, so the team should refer him for help without first talking to him
quiz.explain: Hess, Freudenberg and colleagues found that neutral older faces are read as more emotional than younger ones, because lines and folds resemble expressions. His voice, words and usual pattern tell you far more than his resting face.

quiz.q: What did Williams and colleagues find in their 2009 study of elderspeak in dementia care?
options: Residents were about twice as likely to resist care after elderspeak than after ordinary talk
Residents with dementia could not tell the difference between elderspeak and ordinary talk
Elderspeak made residents calmer and more cooperative than ordinary adult talk did on average
Elderspeak only affected residents without dementia, who found it patronising and disrespectful
quiz.explain: Residents with dementia resisted care about twice as often after elderspeak. Even people with significant cognitive decline heard and responded to being talked down to.

quiz.q: What did the 2011 pooled analysis led by Stephanie Studenski find about older adults?
options: Walking speed had no link to survival once age and sex were taken into account
Older adults who walked slowly were found to have lower scores on tests of memory
Faster walking speed was linked to longer survival across about 34,000 people
Walking speed only predicted survival among older men, and not among older women
quiz.explain: Across nine studies of about 34,000 people over sixty-five, faster gait was linked to longer survival. It is a signal about physical health, not about the mind.

quiz.q: What did Levy and colleagues find in their 2002 study of views of ageing?
options: Views of ageing had no measurable effect on health once income was taken into account
Positive views of ageing were only linked to longevity in people who were already healthy
Negative views of ageing were linked to longer life, because they encouraged more caution
People with more positive views of their own ageing lived about seven and a half years longer
quiz.explain: In the Ohio Longitudinal Study, positive self-perceptions of ageing predicted about seven and a half more years of life. The link held after accounting for age, sex, income, loneliness and health.

quiz.q: Your father, who is hard of hearing, nods along at a family dinner but sometimes answers questions that were not asked. What fits this chapter best?
options: Repeat everything more loudly, so that he can catch each word the second time round
Seat him facing the light, away from noise, and rephrase rather than shout when he misses
Raise the possibility of dementia with him at the table, so that he can be checked quickly
Leave him to enjoy the meal quietly, since joining in is clearly too tiring for him now
quiz.explain: Nodding along and answering the wrong question are classic signs of hearing loss in noise. Position, light and rephrasing help more than volume, which distorts speech.

quiz.q: At work, a younger colleague calls a sixty-six-year-old engineer young man and explains the new software very slowly and loudly. What fits this chapter best?
options: Join in, since older colleagues usually need extra help with new software
Say nothing, since the younger colleague is clearly trying to be helpful
Explain things at a normal pace, and ask him what he already knows first
Suggest to the engineer that he consider retiring before the new system
quiz.explain: Pet names, slow speech and loud volume are elderspeak, and they are usually heard as patronising. Speaking to him as to any adult, and asking what he knows, treats him as the expert he may well be.

quiz.q: In Holt-Lunstad and colleagues' 2010 analysis of 148 studies, what was linked to a greater likelihood of survival?
options: Living alone, which reduced stress from family obligations in later life
Stronger social relationships, linked to about a fifty per cent greater likelihood
Retiring early, which gave people more time to rest and look after themselves
Owning a pet, which was the only social factor that predicted survival at all
quiz.explain: People with stronger social relationships had about a fifty per cent greater likelihood of survival over the study periods. Widowers are often among the most isolated people, which makes this especially relevant to older men.

quiz.q: A carer says to a resident with dementia, in a sing-song voice, "Are we ready for our tablets, sweetheart?" and he pushes her hand away. What fits this chapter best?
options: Record him as resistant to care, since dementia often makes people more difficult
Sit at his level, greet him by name, speak to him as an adult and offer a choice
Speak more slowly and sweetly, since he probably did not understand the first time
Leave the tablets on the table and come back later, since he clearly wants nothing
quiz.explain: Williams and colleagues found residents with dementia were about twice as likely to resist care after elderspeak than after ordinary adult talk. Speaking to him as an adult, at his level, with a choice, respects him and tends to work better.

quiz.q: Someone says shop staff overlook older customers only because older people are slow to come forward. What does this chapter suggest?
options: That younger people pay less attention to older faces, an own-age bias, so the overlooking starts with them
That older customers are always slower to come forward, so the staff are simply responding to that
That shop staff deliberately ignore older customers because they are assumed to spend less money
That being overlooked is something older people imagine, since staff treat all customers the same
quiz.explain: Rhodes and Anastasi's review documented an own-age bias: people attend to and remember faces from their own age group better. Younger staff may simply not see older customers as readily.

reflection.prompt: Think of one specific older man in your life: a father, grandfather, neighbour, colleague or patient. Describe how others treat him in conversation: who addresses him, how they speak to him, where he sits and how often he is asked for his view. Then describe how you treat him. Is there anything in his face, his walk or his hearing that you may have been misreading? What would change if you spoke to him as you would to a man of forty?
reflection.guidance: It can be uncomfortable to notice that you have talked down to someone you love, or left him at the edge of the room. Focus on specific behaviour, such as your pace, volume, words and where you sit, rather than on blame. If you are older yourself, you may write about how you are treated, and what you would like others to do differently.

failureMode: The first failure is to read an older man's resting face as sad or stern, when lines and folds make faces look emotional at rest. The second is to overlook him: to serve the younger customer first, leave him at the edge of the group, or stop asking his view. The third is elderspeak: slow, loud, simplified talk with pet names, which older people hear as patronising and which even people with dementia resist. The fourth is to mistake hearing loss for confusion or rudeness. The fifth is to treat a slower walk as a slower mind. And the sixth is to read the gruffness and withdrawal of a lonely older man as bad temper, and leave him alone.

moreCases.title: The resident who would not take his tablets
moreCases.scene:
Arthur, eighty-six, was a merchant navy engineer for forty years and now lives in a care home with dementia. On good days he talks about ships,
  engines and the ports he worked in, in detail. On bad days he is confused about where he is. Every morning a carer brings him his medication.

  Kayleigh, twenty-two, is new and kind, and she has picked up the way some of the staff talk. She bends down close to his chair and says, in a high,
  sing-song voice, "Morning, sweetheart! Are we ready for our tablets? Good boy, let's take them for me, shall we?" She holds the cup up to his mouth.

  Arthur pushes her hand away. He turns his head, says "Leave me alone" and grips the arms of his chair. Kayleigh tries again, more slowly and more
  sweetly. He knocks the cup to the floor. She writes in his notes that he was "resistant to care" and "agitated", and tells the senior carer that he
  is getting more difficult.

  The senior carer, Mo, fifty, has looked after Arthur for three years. He goes in, sits down in the chair beside him, says "Morning, Arthur, it's Mo,"
  and talks to him for a minute about the weather over the harbour, which Arthur can see from his window. Then he says, plainly, "Here are your morning
  tablets. Would you like them with water or tea?" Arthur says tea, and takes them.

Arthur's daughter, visiting that afternoon, finds the note about agitation and asks what happened. When Mo tells her, she says that her father used to say that the worst thing about the navy was officers who talked to him as if he were stupid.

Kayleigh had learned the voice in her first week from a colleague who used it with every resident. Nobody had told her that it might be the voice, not the dementia, that Arthur was pushing away.

When Mo sits down beside him, Arthur looks at him for a long moment, as if checking who he is, and then visibly relaxes. Mo has noticed that he does this with anyone who sits at his level rather than bending over him.
moreCases.misread:
Kayleigh read Arthur's pushing away and his sharp words as agitation and increasing difficulty, and recorded them as a feature of his dementia. She did not consider that he might be reacting to how he was being spoken to.

The other staff, reading Kayleigh's note, nearly began to treat Arthur as a resident who needed two carers for his medication, which would have been one more indignity.

The note also read his words, "Leave me alone", as part of his illness, when they were a perfectly clear request from an adult who did not want to be spoken to like that.
moreCases.betterRead:
Williams and colleagues found that nursing home residents with dementia were about twice as likely to resist care after staff used elderspeak, with its sing-song tone, pet names and collective "we", than after ordinary adult talk. Even people with dementia heard the difference. Arthur was a man who had run ships' engines; being called "good boy" and fed like a toddler was an insult his illness had not taken away his ability to feel. Mo's approach was the better reading in practice: sit at his level, greet him by name, talk to him as an adult, offer a choice, and let him take the tablets himself. Mo talked to Kayleigh afterwards, without criticism, and showed her the research. She changed how she spoke within a week. Arthur's notes stopped describing him as resistant.

Mo also asked the home to add a short session on elderspeak to its induction for new carers, using Arthur's story with his daughter's permission.

Arthur's daughter told Mo, at the end of the year, that her father always brightened when he heard Mo's voice in the corridor.

moreCases.title: The volunteer everyone thought was grumpy
moreCases.scene:
Bill, seventy, retired from the fire service ten years ago and volunteers three days a week at a charity shop, sorting donations and serving at the
  till. He is a kind, funny man with a great fund of stories. His face, at rest, is another matter. Deep lines run from his nose to the corners of his
  mouth, which turn down, and two vertical furrows sit between his brows. When he is concentrating on the till, he looks, to most people, furious.

  The shop's new manager, Jade, twenty-eight, notices in her first month that customers tend to queue at the other till when Bill is serving, and that
  one or two younger volunteers seem wary of him. She wonders whether Bill is unhappy in the shop, or whether he resents having a younger manager. She
  starts to give him the sorting jobs in the back room rather than the till, without saying why.

  Bill notices. He says nothing, but he starts to come in two days a week instead of three.

  One afternoon Jade hears laughter from the back room and finds Bill telling two of the younger volunteers, in vivid detail, about the night his
  crew rescued a horse from a canal. They are in tears of laughter. Bill's face, telling the story, is entirely different.

Bill has noticed the queue at the other till too. He has assumed the customers prefer the younger volunteer, and has stopped making the small jokes he used to make with regulars.

His wife, when he mentions that he has been moved to the back, says that it has happened before: at his retirement party, a colleague's new wife asked her why Bill looked so cross on such a happy day.

Jade also notices, looking at the rota, that Bill has volunteered every Christmas Eve for six years, which is not the record of a man who is unhappy in the shop.
moreCases.misread:
Jade read Bill's resting face, with its downturned mouth and furrowed brow, as unhappiness or resentment, and the customers read it as unfriendliness. Bill read his move to the back room as a sign that the new manager did not want him at the front.

The younger volunteers who were wary of him had read the same face the same way, and none of them had spent long enough with him to hear him talk.

Jade also read her own decision to move him to the back room as tactful, when it was a judgment about his face made without a word to him.

And the customers who chose the other till read a resting face as a mood, which is how most people read faces they do not know.
moreCases.betterRead:
Hess, Adams and colleagues found that the wrinkles and folds of older faces make expressions less clear, and Freudenberg, Hess and colleagues found that neutral expressions were rated as more emotional on older faces than on younger ones. Lines that follow the paths of decades of expression can look like sadness or anger at rest. Bill's face was simply seventy years old. The better reading, which Jade reached after hearing the laughter, was to judge him by what he did and said rather than by his resting face, and to ask rather than guess. She told him, honestly, that she had wondered whether he was happy in the shop. He laughed and said everyone had always told him he looked cross. She put him back on the till, and on the rota for the shop's school visits, where children asked him about fire engines for an hour.

Jade also mentioned, at the next volunteers' meeting, that faces are poor guides to mood, especially older ones, and told the story of her own mistake.

moreCases.title: The widower next door
moreCases.scene:
Ron, seventy-seven, has lived in the same house for fifty years, and his wife, Margaret, died eighteen months ago. His neighbour, Aisha, thirty-five,
  moved in next door a year ago with her two young children. She sees Ron most days: putting out his bins, collecting his paper, standing at his window.

  When she tries to chat, he is curt. "Morning." "Fine." "Can't complain." When she offers to bring him some shopping, he says he can manage. When her
  children wave to him over the fence, he nods and goes back inside. Aisha's partner says the old man clearly wants to be left alone, and they should
  respect that.

  Aisha is not sure. She has noticed that Ron's curtains often stay closed until midday, that he wears the same cardigan most days, that his garden,
  which a neighbour tells her was once the best on the street, has gone wild. She has also noticed that when the postman stops to talk to him, Ron talks
  for twenty minutes.

  One Saturday, she is struggling to repair a broken fence panel between their gardens. Ron comes out, watches for a moment and says, gruffly, that
  she is doing it wrong. Then he goes inside and comes back with a toolbox.

Aisha has also noticed that he waves, briefly, when her car pulls in at night, as if he has been waiting at the window to see her family home safely.

She has also noticed that he keeps Margaret's coat on the hook by the front door, and that he touches it when he goes out.

On the day of the fence, she notices that he is wearing a clean shirt, and that he has shaved, for the first time in weeks.
moreCases.misread:
Aisha's partner read Ron's curt answers and refusals of help as a wish to be left alone. Ron's refusals were partly pride and partly the habit of a man who did not know how to accept company without a reason.

Ron's curtness was also, partly, a test: whether this new neighbour would keep trying, as Margaret would have wanted him to let her.

And Ron read Aisha's offers of shopping as pity, which made accepting them feel like admitting something about himself that he was not ready to admit.

Aisha's partner, who worked long hours and rarely saw Ron, read him from a few curt exchanges at the bins.
moreCases.betterRead:
Holt-Lunstad and colleagues found that people with stronger social relationships had about a fifty per cent greater likelihood of survival, and research on later life repeatedly finds widowers among the most isolated people of all. This chapter describes how loneliness in older men often shows as gruffness, letting appearance go and long silences broken by bursts of talk, which are easily read as bad temper. Ron's toolbox was the opening. Aisha's better response was the Side by Side drill: she accepted his help, let him show her how to fix the fence and asked whether he would help her with the garden too. Over the following months, Ron spent Saturday mornings helping her and teaching her children to plant beans. His curtains started opening earlier. When Aisha later mentioned that he seemed low some days, he agreed to see his GP, and started going to a bereavement group at the library.

Aisha's children started calling him Uncle Ron, which he pretended to find annoying.

The garden, by the following summer, was back to something like its old state, and Ron entered the street's flower show.

moreCases.title: The customer in the phone shop
moreCases.scene:
George, eighty-one, walks with a frame since a hip replacement last year. He goes into a phone shop on the high street because his phone has
  stopped syncing with his laptop. He moves slowly to the counter, leans on the frame and waits while the young assistant, Josh, finishes serving
  someone else.

  When Josh turns to him, he speaks slowly and loudly, and says, "What can I do for you today, sir? Is it your phone? Is it the buttons?" When George
  explains that the phone is no longer syncing with his laptop's calendar after an update, Josh says, "Right, OK, so the calendar is like a diary on the
  phone," and begins to explain what a calendar is. He suggests that George might find a simpler phone easier, and shows him one with large buttons.

  George waits until Josh has finished. Then he explains, precisely, that he spent thirty-five years as a software engineer, that he wrote part of the
  operating system for a bank's first cash machines, and that the problem is almost certainly a change in the authentication settings in the last update.

  Josh goes red. He checks the settings, finds that George is right, and fixes it in two minutes.

George has had the same experience at the bank, the GP's surgery and the railway station, and has learned to wait until people finish before correcting them, because it saves time in the end.

He had come in, he says later, partly because he wanted to see how long it would take the shop to work out that he knew what he was talking about.

Josh, in his defence, had been trained to "keep it simple" with customers, and nobody had told him that simple and patronising are not the same.
moreCases.misread:
Josh read George's frame, slow walk and age as signs that he would not understand technology, and talked to him slowly, loudly and simply. He read a problem about software settings as a problem about buttons.

The customer behind George in the queue, a man in his thirties, had read the same frame the same way, and was visibly surprised by the conversation that followed.

George, for his part, read Josh's manner accurately, as a young man who meant well and had not been taught otherwise, and decided to be patient rather than offended.
moreCases.betterRead:
Studenski and colleagues found that walking speed is a genuine health signal, linked to survival in older adults, but it is a signal about the body, not the mind. Wright's idea of spread, described in the previous chapter, applies here: a slow walk was taken as a sign that George was less capable in every way, including the one in which he was more expert than anyone in the shop. Josh's elderspeak, the slow, loud, simplified talk with "sir" and a description of what a calendar is, made the mistake audible. The better approach would have been the Adult to Adult drill: speak to him as you would to any customer of forty, listen to the problem he describes and take the description at face value. Josh apologised, and George laughed and told him about the cash machines for ten minutes. Josh told his manager it was the best customer he had had all month.

Josh's manager added a line to the shop's training: ask customers what they already know before explaining anything.

workedReading.title: Bringing an experienced colleague into a change
workedReading.scene:
Natalie, thirty-one, has just become manager of a team of six surveyors at a property firm, and the firm is moving all its surveys from paper forms to a tablet app. The most experienced member of the team is Stan, sixty-four, who has been surveying buildings for forty years and is respected by every builder in the county. Natalie has heard from others that Stan is "not a tech person" and will resist the change. She has also noticed, in her first few weeks, that in team meetings people tend to talk across Stan to each other, and that he has stopped offering his views. She wants him to be part of the change, not someone it is done to, and she suspects that how she speaks to him will matter as much as what she says. She decides to start by checking her own assumptions.

She also remembers her own grandfather, a carpenter, who was given a computer by his children and taught himself to design furniture on it at seventy-five. She suspects the label "not a tech person" may say more about the people using it than about Stan.

She has also seen, in her last job, a long-serving colleague retire early after a reorganisation in which nobody asked his opinion, and she does not want to repeat it.

steps.label: Check your own assumptions
steps.text:
Before speaking to Stan, she writes down what she believes about him: that he will struggle with the app, that he will resist it, that he will need extra help. Then she asks what evidence she has. She has none of her own; it is all what others have said. She remembers the chapter's warning about spread: a man's age and the length of his career say nothing about his ability to learn a new tool.

She also notices that two of the younger surveyors are much less confident with the app than they let on, and that nobody has described them as not tech people.

She also notices that she has been planning to give Stan the training first, alone, to save him embarrassment, and realises that this plan rested on the same unexamined assumption.

steps.label: Talk adult to adult
steps.text:
She asks Stan for half an hour, one to one, in a quiet room. She speaks to him at the same pace and in the same words she would use with any colleague, without "Don't worry" or "It's really easy" or any of the softening that would tell him she expects him to find it hard. She explains what the change is, why the firm is making it and when it will happen, and asks what he thinks.

She also avoids standing over him or perching on the desk. They sit across a corner of the table, at the same height.

She also says, plainly, that she would value his view more than anyone's, because he knows the work best. It is true, and it sets the tone for the rest of the conversation.

steps.label: Ask his view first
steps.text:
Stan says, after a pause, that the app looks fine but that it does not have a way to record the condition of roof timbers the way surveyors actually look at them, which means the reports will be worse. He has looked at the demo version on his own phone already. Natalie had not known that the app had that gap, and had not known that he had looked at it. She writes it down.

She thanks him, and asks whether he would be willing to raise it in the training, which he says he would.

She also asks him what else he thinks the firm should know about the change, and he gives her two practical suggestions about working in poor signal on rural sites.

steps.label: Set up the training room
steps.text:
For the team training session, she makes sure the room is quiet, the tablets have large screens and the trainer faces the group rather than the projector. She asks the trainer to explain the app as he would to any group of professionals, and to take questions from everyone. She sits next to Stan rather than at the front, so that she can see whether anything is unclear for anyone at that end of the table.

She also asks the trainer not to single out anyone for extra help, but to offer a follow-up session to the whole team.

She also books the session in the morning rather than late in the afternoon, which suits everyone's concentration better.

steps.label: Credit his experience publicly
steps.text:
During the training, when the trainer reaches the section on roofs, Natalie says, "Stan spotted a problem with this part. Stan, can you explain?" Stan explains the issue clearly, and the trainer agrees to pass it to the developers. The younger surveyors, several of whom had not noticed the gap, listen to him with obvious respect.

She also notices that Stan sits up straighter after he has explained, and offers two more comments during the session, more than he has said in any meeting since she arrived.

She also makes sure the credit goes in writing, in her notes to the developers, with his name on the suggestion.

steps.label: Talk to him, not around him
steps.text:
In the following weeks, when team discussions start to flow across Stan, Natalie turns to him and asks what he thinks, then waits. She notices that once she does it a few times, others start to do it too. The Seen Less block of this chapter describes how older men are overlooked in groups; she has found that a single person turning towards them changes the pattern for everyone.

She also starts meetings by asking a different person for their view each time, which spreads the attention without making anyone the special case.

She also notices that she had been doing it herself in her first weeks, talking across him to the younger surveyors, without meaning to.

steps.label: What happened
steps.text:
The developers add a roof-timber section to the app, and the firm credits Stan in the release notes. Stan becomes the person the younger surveyors ask when the app does something odd on site, because he has learned it more thoroughly than anyone. At the end of the year, he tells Natalie that she was the first manager in a decade who had asked his opinion before telling him what was going to happen.

She also passes the story to her own manager, who asks Stan to help design the firm's training for new surveyors.

She also notices how much more she learns from the team when Stan is talking, because he knows the history of every building in the county.

moreFailures.title: Making age the joke
moreFailures.body:
"Senior moment," "old boy," "past it," "back in your day," "OK, granddad": jokes about age are among the few kinds of teasing that remain broadly acceptable in many workplaces and families, and older men are often expected to laugh along. Some do, and some genuinely enjoy the banter. But age jokes do quiet work. They frame forgetfulness, slowness or unfamiliarity with something new as signs of age rather than as ordinary human lapses that happen to everyone, and they tell younger people in the room how older colleagues are seen. Levy's research suggests that the stereotypes people absorb about ageing can shape their own health as they get older, so the jokes may also land, years later, on the people making them. If a forty-year-old forgets a name, nobody calls it a senior moment. Try holding older colleagues to the same standard.

If you enjoy the banter yourself, ask whether the older colleague is laughing because he finds it funny or because it is expected.

It also helps to notice whether the older colleague is ever the one making the jokes, or only their subject.

moreFailures.title: Assuming technology is beyond him
moreFailures.body:
Many people assume that older men cannot use, or do not want to use, smartphones, apps, video calls and computers, and treat them accordingly: explaining basics they already know, doing things for them, offering simpler devices, leaving them out of digital changes, as Josh did with George. Some older men do find new technology frustrating; so do many younger ones. But the generation now in their sixties, seventies and eighties includes the engineers, programmers and technicians who built much of the technology in use today, and many older people use it confidently every day. The assumption is a form of spread, from age to ability. The fix is simple: ask what someone already knows and how they would like to proceed, then explain at the level they ask for, as you would with anyone.

A good question to ask is "How do you usually do this?", which tells you where to start and treats him as competent.

moreFailures.title: Helping without asking
moreFailures.body:
The previous chapter described how unasked-for help, taking an arm, carrying a bag, pushing a wheelchair, removes control from a disabled person. The same applies to older men, who are often helped without being asked: taken by the elbow across a road, steered onto a bus, relieved of their shopping, guided to a seat. Each act is usually meant kindly. Each also says, without words, that the helper has judged the older man unable to manage, and many men feel that judgment sharply, especially those who were strong and independent for most of their lives. Ask first: "Would you like a hand?" Then accept the answer, including a no. Holding a door, offering a seat and walking at someone's pace are courtesies; taking someone's arm without asking is not.

And if he says no, do not hover nearby waiting for him to fail. Trust the answer.

If you are unsure whether he would welcome help, offering a choice works well: "I'm going that way, would you like company?"

moreFailures.title: Reading your own ageing as decline
moreFailures.body:
This chapter is mostly about how others read older men, but the same readings can be turned inward. Many men in their fifties and sixties start to read their own bodies through the stereotypes they have absorbed: every ache is the beginning of the end, every forgotten word a sign of decline, every grey hair a reason to step back. Levy and colleagues found that people with more positive views of their own ageing lived about seven and a half years longer than those with more negative views, after accounting for health and other factors. The research does not show that optimism alone keeps people alive, and some of the studies behind it are small. But it suggests that how you think about your own ageing is not neutral. Noticing the stereotype in your own head, and checking it against the evidence, is worth doing for yourself as well as for others.

It also helps to notice older men you admire, and how they carry themselves, as a counterweight to the stereotype.

If you find yourself saying "I'm too old for that", ask whether it is true or just a story you have absorbed.

questions.q: How can I tell whether an older man is unhappy or just has a serious resting face?
questions.a:
Often you cannot tell from the face alone, and you should not try. Hess, Adams and colleagues found that the lines and folds of older faces make expressions less clear, and Freudenberg, Hess and colleagues found that neutral older faces were read as more emotional than neutral younger ones. A mouth that turns down at rest, or furrows between the brows, can look like sadness or anger when the man feels neither. So look at other signals: what he says, how he says it, what he does, how he behaves with people he knows. Read him against his own baseline, as Jade eventually did with Bill. If you are genuinely concerned that someone is unhappy, ask in an ordinary way: "How are you doing?" and listen to the answer, rather than deciding from his face.

If he seems genuinely low, it is worth asking more than once, on different days, since many older men answer the first question with "Fine" by habit.

questions.q: What is wrong with calling an older man "young man" or "sweetheart"?
questions.a:
Usually nothing is meant by it except friendliness, but it is a form of elderspeak, the way of talking to older people as if they were children that researchers such as Susan Kemper have described. Pet names, the collective "we", a sing-song voice, slow and loud speech and over-simple explanations are often heard as patronising, and Williams and colleagues found that even people with dementia resisted care more after staff used elderspeak. "Young man" to a man of eighty also makes his age the joke. The respectful alternative is ordinary adult speech: his name or "sir" if that is the setting's norm, your normal pace and volume, and whatever words you would use with a man of forty. If he cannot hear you, face him and speak clearly; do not switch to baby talk.

It also helps to notice if you slip into it under pressure, for example when you are in a hurry or he has not understood.

questions.q: How can I tell whether hearing loss is the problem?
questions.a:
Look for the patterns this chapter describes: nodding along but answering a different question, laughing a beat late, leaning in, turning one ear towards the speaker, watching lips closely, asking people to repeat themselves, avoiding noisy places or withdrawing in groups. These are easily read as confusion, rudeness or disinterest. If you notice them, adjust the setting: sit him facing the light, away from noise, and speak clearly without shouting, rephrasing rather than repeating. Then, if it seems appropriate, suggest a hearing test gently and practically: "It's so noisy in here, I can barely hear either. Have you had your hearing checked lately?" The World Health Organization estimates that more than a quarter of people over sixty have a disabling hearing loss, so it is a common and treatable cause of apparent withdrawal.

It also helps to know that untreated hearing loss can increase isolation, so a test is worth encouraging gently but firmly.

questions.q: My father has become gruff and withdrawn since my mother died. What can I do?
questions.a:
Keep showing up, and try doing things side by side rather than face to face. Many older men find it hard to talk about grief or loneliness directly, but easier to talk while fixing something, gardening, walking, watching a match or cooking together, as Ron did with Aisha's fence. Invite him to help with a task rather than offering to help him, which respects his independence. Make it regular, since one visit rarely changes much. Encourage connections outside the family, such as a club, a Men's Shed or a volunteering role. If his low mood persists for weeks, if he stops eating or looking after himself, or if he talks about not wanting to go on, encourage him to see his GP, and in an emergency get help immediately. Holt-Lunstad and colleagues' work suggests that social connection matters for health as well as happiness.

It can also help to let him look after you sometimes, for example by asking his advice, which restores a role grief may have taken.

questions.q: Does a slow walk mean someone is frail?
questions.a:
It may say something about his physical health. Studenski and colleagues found that walking speed was linked to survival in older adults, and doctors increasingly treat it as a vital sign. But it says nothing about his mind, his knowledge or his ability to make decisions, and reading it that way is the mistake Josh made with George. A man who walks with a frame after a hip operation may be the sharpest person in the room. The respectful response to a slow walk is practical: walk at his pace and beside him rather than half a step ahead, hold doors without hurrying him, choose routes without too many stairs if he wants that, and otherwise treat him exactly as you would anyone else.

It also helps not to finish his errands for him unless he asks; independence often matters more than speed.

And if he is walking with someone younger, address him, not his companion, when you ask the way or offer help.

questions.q: How can I carry myself well as I get older?
questions.a:
Keep moving, keep connected and watch the stories you tell yourself. Levy and colleagues found that people with more positive views of their own ageing lived longer, after accounting for health and other factors, though the research does not show that attitude alone is the cause. Regular walking, strength and balance exercise and staying active help the body. Staying in regular contact with others, through work, volunteering, clubs or family, helps both health and mood. Get your hearing and eyesight checked, so that you do not withdraw from conversations without meaning to. And notice the age stereotypes in your own head, the senior moments and the past-its, and check them against the evidence as you would anyone else's.

And remember that older age is a long stretch of life, not a single stage. Most people in it are still learning.

It also helps to spend time with people of different ages, which keeps your own picture of ageing more accurate.
